title: Cooley CEO: Big Law Won't Survive if It Treats AI as Just an Efficiency Tool
author: Rachel Proffitt

dom.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Proffitt accepts the cluster’s core claim that AI requires organisational and business-model redesign rather than isolated efficiency gains. She materially extends it from the law-firm perspective by linking redesign to value-based pricing, workflows, talent models and deliberate experimentation, while predicting uneven competitive outcomes. She does not, however, substantiate the cluster’s buyer-side adoption or gain-capture claims with quantitative evidence.
qs: Those that embrace it can redesign the business of law.
That means engaging in deliberate experimentation, accepting some trial and error around service delivery, pricing, workflows, and talent models.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Proffitt accepts that AI-driven efficiency can destabilise existing law-firm structures without destroying the legal industry, and materially extends the cluster by arguing that firms must redesign pricing and delivery around client outcomes rather than merely automate work within the billable-hour model. Her contribution is strategic and predictive, not empirical evidence of staffing or market-wide effects.
qs: Law firms that treat AI merely as an efficiency gain risk weakening the very model that sustained them.
For generations, the billable hour, the foundation of our business model, offered a clear measure of input – but input is not what clients value – clients value outcomes.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that firms must redesign their operating models and client value propositions rather than treat AI merely as an efficiency tool. It aligns particularly on value-based pricing, shifting lawyers toward judgment and trusted relationships, and adapting recruitment and training, while offering strategic predictions rather than new empirical evidence about agentic systems or Harvey’s durability.
qs: Pricing must increasingly reflect value created rather than time spent, whether tied to business or legal outcomes, risk mitigation, speed, or greater predictability.
This shift will transform how we recruit, train, and retain the next generation of practitioners.

kp.k: AI challenges Big Law’s historically stable business model
kp.d: Proffitt characterizes legal business models, pricing, and career paths as historically stable and reinforced by market visibility, consensus, and precedent. She argues that AI represents a foundational rather than incremental disruption that scale or spending alone cannot address. These are assertions in a leadership commentary, not findings supported by a reported empirical study.
qs: Our core business models, pricing structures, and career paths have endured largely unaltered, even as other industries evolved around us.
It is a model built on consensus and precedent rather than innovation, and for a long time, it has worked.
This is not another incremental advance in technology or a problem to be solved with scale or spend.

kp.k: Efficiency-only adoption risks weakening firms rather than renewing them
kp.d: Proffitt rejects predictions that AI will undermine the entire legal industry. Instead, she forecasts uneven outcomes depending on firms’ responses: treating AI merely as an efficiency improvement risks weakening their existing model, whereas embracing broader change creates an opportunity to redesign legal businesses.
qs: Some seem to be predicting an upheaval that will undermine the entire industry. I think they have it wrong.
Law firms that treat AI merely as an efficiency gain risk weakening the very model that sustained them.
Those that embrace it can redesign the business of law.

kp.k: Client outcomes should replace time as pricing’s primary basis
kp.d: Proffitt asserts that clients increasingly prioritize speed, certainty, and alignment with business outcomes, exposing a mismatch between hourly billing’s measurement of inputs and what clients value. She recommends pricing around outcomes, risk mitigation, speed, and predictability, and predicts that time will cease to be the primary measure of value. She qualifies this prediction by noting that adoption speeds will vary, without specifying a timetable.
qs: The divide is already emerging and increasingly widening as clients place greater emphasis on speed, certainty, and alignment with business outcomes.
Pricing must increasingly reflect value created rather than time spent, whether tied to business or legal outcomes, risk mitigation, speed, or greater predictability.
The pace of adoption will vary but the direction of travel is clear.
Time spent will lose its place as the industry’s primary measure of value.

kp.k: Routine-task automation requires changes to lawyer development
kp.d: Proffitt asserts that AI is already absorbing repeatable tasks that historically supported both service execution and lawyer training. She argues that this shifts where lawyers contribute value rather than eliminating the need for them, while requiring the talent model to evolve. She anticipates changes in recruitment, training, and retention but does not specify staffing ratios, headcount effects, or replacement training mechanisms.
qs: AI has begun absorbing routine, repeatable tasks, the work that for decades underpinned both execution and training.
This does not eliminate the need for lawyers, but it redefines where lawyers create value by allowing us to spend more time where clients need us most.
This also foreshadows the difficult reality that our talent model must evolve in tandem.
This shift will transform how we recruit, train, and retain the next generation of practitioners.

kp.k: Judgment and client trust differentiate AI-enabled lawyers
kp.d: Proffitt argues that clients’ emphasis on who solves their business problems elevates lawyers’ judgment and relationships. Her proposed model combines human expertise and client trust with increasingly capable AI, rather than dispensing with lawyers. She predicts that successful next-generation practitioners will embrace technology alongside the profession’s best traditions.
qs: That distinction elevates judgment and the relationships lawyers build with their clients.
Successful firms will be those who combine technology with expertise and client trust to solve clients’ most complex challenges.
The goal is to layer the best human intelligence over an increasingly powerful AI technology stack.

kp.k: New entrants intensify incumbents’ transition challenge
kp.d: Proffitt describes competition as extending beyond incumbent law firms to legal-tech companies and AI-native firms. She identifies the central challenge for established firms as maintaining successful businesses under current structures while building for changed conditions. She expects this transition to be uneven and not coordinated through industry consensus.
qs: No longer just a race among law firm incumbents, legal tech companies and AI-native firms enter the field almost daily.
Established law firms must continue to run successful businesses built on today’s structures while architecting for a tomorrow that is already here.
This transition will not happen all at once, nor by industry consensus.

kp.k: Leadership should experiment across pricing, workflows, and talent
kp.d: Proffitt attributes law-firm leaders’ slow engagement to uncertainty and argues that continued conservatism risks surrendering control over the profession’s future. She recommends deliberate experimentation and tolerance for trial and error across service delivery, pricing, workflows, and talent models. Her commitment to transform Cooley is a stated intention, not evidence of implemented changes or measured results.
qs: Big Law leaders have been slow to engage because so much is unknown.
That conservatism no longer serves our profession – if we fail to act now, the future will be decided for us rather than by us.
That means engaging in deliberate experimentation, accepting some trial and error around service delivery, pricing, workflows, and talent models.

I am fully committing Cooley to this shift – not fearfully approaching AI as a set of tools but embracing it as an opportunity to transform our business and how we deliver value in the modern economy.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rachel Proffitt predicts a fundamental, uneven restructuring of Big Law, not the disappearance of the entire legal industry.
pts.d: Proffitt argues that established operating models cannot endure unchanged. Firms that approach AI only as an efficiency tool risk weakening their existing business model, whereas firms that embrace broader transformation can redesign their businesses. She explicitly rejects the prediction that disruption will undermine the entire industry.

pts.k: Proffitt predicts that time spent will cease to be the primary measure of legal-service value as pricing shifts toward outcomes.
pts.d: She claims AI exposes the mismatch between hourly inputs and clients' priorities: speed, certainty, business alignment, risk mitigation and predictability. Her prediction is a declining primacy of time-based valuation, not an explicit claim that all hourly billing will disappear.

pts.k: Proffitt says AI is already absorbing routine legal tasks, changing where lawyers contribute value and requiring changes to talent development.
pts.d: She presents AI as augmenting lawyers rather than eliminating the need for them. Because routine tasks historically supported both execution and training, their absorption by AI requires changes in recruitment, training and retention. She does not specify headcount reductions, a future staffing shape or a replacement training model.

pts.k: Proffitt predicts that judgment, expertise and client trust will become central differentiators when combined with AI.
pts.d: She argues that clients prioritize who can solve their business problems over how the work is performed. Her envisioned successful firm combines human expertise and relationships with increasingly powerful technology. She describes AI as an equalizer while predicting that leading next-generation lawyers will distinguish themselves through both technology adoption and traditional professional strengths.

pts.k: Proffitt claims competition now extends beyond incumbent law firms and requires experimentation while existing businesses continue operating.
pts.d: She identifies legal-tech companies and AI-native firms as entrants, without specifying their business models or quantifying their market share. Established firms face a dual obligation to sustain current operations and build new structures. She advocates experimentation in delivery, pricing, workflows and talent, and commits Cooley to transformation; this commitment is not evidence of completed implementation or demonstrated results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on Proffitt's executive perspective, qualitative industry observations and experience advising innovative companies.
pts.d: This is commentary attributed to Cooley CEO Rachel Proffitt. She offers observations about client preferences, routine-task automation, competitive entry and leadership conservatism, and invokes her firm's advisory experience. The document supplies no quantitative data, benchmarks, named client cases, measured productivity or pricing outcomes, or external studies supporting the predictions. Fortune identifies the opinions as the author's own.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Proffitt describes disruption as already underway in the 2026 commentary, with urgent but gradual and uneven adaptation ahead.
pts.d: Routine-task absorption and competitive change are presented as current developments. Pricing, talent and business-model transformation are forward-looking, with no specified completion date. Adoption will vary, and transition will occur neither simultaneously nor through industry consensus. Firm success is conditioned on combining technology with expertise and trust and pursuing broader redesign rather than efficiency alone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Big Law firms and leaders, clients, current and future lawyers, and emerging competitors.
pts.d: Incumbent firms face changes to pricing, service delivery, workflows, talent models and competitive positioning; leaders must maintain current operations while experimenting. Clients' business outcomes, speed, certainty and trust become the proposed basis of value. Lawyers shift away from routine execution toward judgment and relationships, while future practitioners face redesigned development and expectations of technological fluency. Legal-tech companies and AI-native firms broaden the competitive field. Cooley is expressly committed to this shift. The document makes no specific claims about access to justice, public legal need or particular non-lawyer occupations.
